node.label: Carl Berger
node.date_label: The Sense of Power 1970 · The Writing of Canadian History 1976; 2nd ed. 1986
node.description: A University of Toronto historian of English-Canadian ideas. The Sense of Power (1970) is 'a study in Canadian nationalist thought': against the 'so-called liberal nationalist school', for which imperialism and nationalism added up to 'a struggle between the past and the future', he argued that 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission'. The Writing of Canadian History (1976; second edition 1986) examines 'aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century' through the 'central teachings' of Wrong, Shortt, Martin, Innis, Lower, Underhill, Creighton and Morton, and treats written history as 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; he left French-Canadian writing aside because the two language traditions had been 'preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”'. In period, Jacques Monet thought the imperialism thesis 'très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (1972), while Douglas Cole and Graham Carr held that it over-Canadianized a Britannic movement, Susan Mann Trofimenkoff called his imperialists' nationalism 'decidedly masculine' (1979), Allen Mills found that his account of all Canadian historians as nationalists put 'much too much weight on that over-used term' (1977), and Ronald Rudin rejected his assumption that historians were 'united by their search for the truth' (1997).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Carl Berger (b. 1939); ed., Imperialism and Nationalism, 1884–1914: A Conflict in Canadian Thought (1969); The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (1970; 2nd ed. 2013, with an introduction by Doug Owram); The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (1976; 2nd ed., … since 1900, 1986, with a new chapter, 'Tradition and the “New” History'); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983). Readings: Monet (1972); Mills (1977); Terry Cook (1977–78); Trofimenkoff (1979); Carr (1982); Karr (1989); Rudin (1997). Later reading: Owram (2013).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the two framework books. Neither could be read continuously: both are borrow-only on the Internet Archive. Berger's own words are quoted from Google Books snippet views (The Sense of Power, 2013 printing with the 1970 pagination: introduction pp. 3, 9–10, conclusion p. 259; The Writing of Canadian History, 1986 edition: both prefaces and pp. 181, 261–262, 289, 298, 312), and are corroborated by in-period reviews read in full: Monet (1972), Mills (1977) and Terry Cook (1977–78). Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983) is checked at metadata level only. He is not presented as the originator of the imperialism thesis: Monet notes that Norman Penlington's Canada and Imperialism (1965) had already suggested it. Contested in period: Page, Cole and Nelles (1970, as Monet reports them), Cole (1971), Carr (1982, journal abstract), Karr (1989) on the elite group-biography method, Trofimenkoff (1979) on women, and Rudin (1997) on French-Canadian writing and on the assumption of a common search for truth. No in-period text found here faults The Writing of Canadian History for treating only male historians; Trofimenkoff's critique is of the field. Owram's 2013 introduction is a later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Canadian imperialism read as one form of Canadian nationalism, through the ideas of its leading spokesmen (1970)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3). Of the earlier critics he writes that 'When critics belaboured imperialism because of its hostility to “Canadian nationalism” what they really meant was that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed. There have been many varieties of Canadian nationalism'; imperialism was 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission' (p. 9). His method: 'inquiring into the ideas and ideals which men in the past read into their interpretations of Canada and by exploring the relationship between these conceptions and the environment in which they circulated' (p. 10). The conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). In-period reception. Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, pp. 274–276, read in full): the book's 'grande originalité' is to conclude that the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (p. 275); the book is 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' (p. 276). Monet also reports the first criticisms (p. 275 and nn. 2–4): neglect of the economic and military sides of imperialism (Robert Page, JCS 1970), the folding into a Canadianizing ideology of witnesses 'qui seraient plutôt des représentants du pan-britannisme' (Douglas Cole, JCS 1970), and too much weight on 'une petite élite' of intellectuals (H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum 1970); Page, Cole (1970) and Nelles are not read here. Cole's 1971 comparative article (notes read; body closed) says that Berger 'makes the strongest case for a Canadian nationalistic consciousness within these terms' (n. 33). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979, read): he 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists', but 'Their nationalism and their imperialism were, however, decidedly masculine affairs' (p. 10); intellectual history 'will have to take women into account' (p. 10). Clarence Karr (1989, re-read): Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' (p. 161); 'Carl Berger's critics accuse him of an over-Canadianization of imperialism and of ignoring a broader Anglo-Saxon perspective in what Graham Carr refers to as a “scavenger hunt for nationalism”' (pp. 162–163); since his book, group biography 'has been upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method of addressing the Canadian intellectual tradition' (p. 167), and its premise that imperialism can 'only be understood in relation to the characters who espoused it and who came to personify it' risks making thought 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe' (p. 168). Carr's article (JCS 1982) is checked at its journal abstract only. A contribution, not an origin: Monet credits Penlington with the suggestion. Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Doug Owram's introduction to the 2013 edition (snippet view) calls it 'pretty much the standard interpretation of the way in which Canadian nationalism evolved' (p. xi).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: empire_and_nation ('Ideas of empire, nation and history') names Berger and cites cic_berger_1970; its focus is exactly the checked thesis. The sibling Cook draft (pe135_cook_rel_07) targets the same strand for Cook's own critique of nationalism; the two arrows carry different claims. The critiques strand (Trofimenkoff, Karr) is not targeted: those critics are recorded in the evidence.

proposed_edges.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: analysing_tradition ('The tradition as historiography') opens with Berger's book and names him. edge_824 (cdn_intellectual_cultural → cdn_national_tradition) currently carries the same book at title level; see the optional relabel in edge_revisions.

proposed_edges.relationship: The liberal nationalist account of imperialism as a colonial past defeated by Canadian nationalism, criticised (1970)
proposed_edges.map_label: Against the liberal nationalist reading of imperialism, 1970
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The interpretation he set out to revise: 'The conflict between imperialism and nationalism added up to a struggle between the past and the future, the desire to remain a colony and the wish to be a free nation. Once this framework was accepted, it was easy to account for the failure of imperialism: it succumbed to Canadian nationalism. The main outlines of this interpretation survived largely because of the great influence of O. D. Skelton's biography of Laurier and because of the long dominance of a particular school of Canadian historiography of which it was the finest expression. This so-called liberal nationalist school has lately come under some penetrating scrutiny, its insufficiencies have been exposed and its continued relevance questioned. Naturally, its interpretation of imperialism has also been found wanting, at least by implication' (p. 9). Against it he argued that critics who attacked imperialism for 'its hostility to “Canadian nationalism”' 'really meant that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed' (p. 9). In-period corroboration that this was the received English-Canadian view: Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, read in full) writes that the imperialists 'ont eu très mauvaise presse parmi les historiens du Canada' and that English-Canadian historians, 'partisans pour la plupart de l'explication de l'équipe gagnante', saw them as 'des conservateurs retardataires' (p. 274); Berger 'vient maintenant nuancer ces jugements... téméraires' (p. 274). The same judgement runs into his historiography: in The Writing of Canadian History (1976) the main criticism of English-Canadian historians, as Allen Mills reads it (1977, read), is that they wrote 'as if they were contributing to pressing matters of contemporary public concern, especially the matter of national survival' (Mills's words, pp. 135–136). A counter-critique: Graham Carr (JCS 1982; journal abstract only) argues that 'revisionists such as Carl Berger, while ostensibly challenging Whig assumptions about imperialism/nationalism, actually share many of the traditional views'. The arrow records Berger's criticism of a position, the liberal nationalist account of imperialism; it does not claim that the national-tradition historians shared one view, and Skelton, whom he names, has no atlas entry.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand (Sol 1.136 finding 7): liberal_conservative_nationalists also holds the conservative nationalists, and Berger's p. 9 names the 'so-called liberal nationalist school' through Skelton's Laurier, not Lower or Underhill. The target is stated in the relationship and evidence note.
proposed_edges.include_note: Included because the brief asks for critique edges where the person criticised an atlas entry's position in his own words. His words are a snippet witness (not read continuously); Monet's full-text review independently confirms that the book overturned the received English-Canadian view.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. The Writing of Canadian History has a chapter 'Harold Innis: The Search for Limits' (pp. 85–111; snippet view: 'To turn from Underhill to Innis is to take leave of the more negative and iconoclastic temper of the twenties and thirties and move toward that period's creative centre', p. 85). It is a historiographical portrait, cited as such by Salmon (1997, n. 2, for 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory') and Kealey (1995, p. 155, n. 7). The atlas has no 'reading of' kind: it is neither an influence on Berger nor a critique of Innis. A source addendum to the Innis entry would be the right place if reviewers want it.

Not proposed. edge_821 (cdn_intellectual_cultural → nationalismstudies, comparison) already cites Berger's chapters and says the Canadian works rarely engage the theory debates. Cole's comparative article (Journal of British Studies, 1971) engages the thesis across settlement colonies, but its body is closed and it is imperial history, not one of the entry's theorists. Kaufmann's 1998 articles on Canadian naturalistic nationalism (CSSH; Nations and Nationalism) might cite Berger's 'True North' essay; both PDFs were blocked, so unchecked.

Not proposed. His method statement (1970, p. 10) is a history of ideas in their environment, but no in-period text checked here ties him to the entry's strands (Lovejoy, Cambridge contextualism, Koselleck). edge_819 (comparison) records that the Canadian field developed largely apart from them. Owram's 2013 introduction places the book against Lovejoy's history of ideas (p. xx, snippet), but that is a later reading.

Lead, not proposed. The 1986 chapter speaks to fragmentation before the 1990s debate: social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298), and 'few historians have paused to consider the relationship of the findings of the new and old histories' (p. 318, snippet). He has no roster row there, the evidence is a snippet witness, and no reviewer reading was found. The sibling Careless draft (pe135_careless_rel_05) already carries the limited-identities-to-fragmentation line into this entry.

Not proposed. His exclusion of French-Canadian writing is explained in his preface and p. 181, and Rudin's criticism is recorded on edge 2. edge_799 (cdn_national_tradition — quebec_historiography, comparison) already notes that Berger's subtitle restricts his subject to English-Canadian writing. A critique edge would run from Rudin's side, not Berger's.

Not proposed. The 1986 chapter summarises the labour-history debate as 'captious, intemperate, and confusing' (p. 306) between 'the upholders of the social democratic tradition and those who had embraced a humanistic Marxism' (pp. 306–307, as quoted by Kealey). Kealey (1995, p. 18) accepts the overall assessment and notes that it 'conforms closely to Bercuson's own view' (p. 30, n. 68). A summary of a field is not a contribution to it.

Not proposed. The 1983 lectures are metadata-checked only (cic_berger_1983); he has no roster row on cdn_religion_reform, and the victorian_thought strand of cdn_intellectual_cultural already holds the book.

proposed.relationship: Historical writing treated as a domain of English-Canadian intellectual history and its national preoccupation examined (1971–86)
proposed.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Trofimenkoff (1979, p. 9, read): 'some of the people have suggested that the leit motiv of both English and French Canadian historical writing, in itself a domain of intellectual history, has been the concern for survival, a nationalist concern'; her note 4 cites Ramsay Cook's essays 'La Survivance French Canadian Style' and 'La Survivance English Canadian Style' in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 114–40, 141–65; not read here). Karr (1989, p. 161, read) places Berger's analysis of 'the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote' among the English-Canadian intellectual historians' studies of nationalism. Berger's 1986 chapter records that 'J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261, snippet view). The arrow records intellectual historians making the national tradition's writing an object of study; Berger's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (the Canadian persons Tier 1 revision).

cic_berger_1970.note: Thesis checked in Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read. Introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3); 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission', and the critique of the 'so-called liberal nationalist school' and of Skelton's Laurier (p. 9); method (p. 10). Conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). So both words occur: 'variety' (p. 9) and 'form' (p. 259). First edition: Monet's and Mills's reviews give University of Toronto Press, 1970 (277 pp.); Karr cites 1971.

cic_berger_1976.note: Checked in Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read. 1976 contents: '10. William Morton: The Delicate Balance of Region and Nation 238; 11. Conclusion 259; Bibliographical Note 265; Notes 267; Index 292'. 1986 contents: chapter 1 'The Founders of Critical History: George M. Wrong and Adam Shortt' 1; 'Harold Innis: The Search for Limits' pp. 85–111; new chapter 'Tradition and the “New” History' from p. 259. Quoted: preface ('This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century'; the eight 'major figures'; 'creative edge'; 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; 'two rather different “nations”'); preface to the second edition ('dispensed with the short conclusion'; 'vast exfoliation'); pp. 181, 261, 262 (Careless 1969 quoted), 289, 298, 312. The 1976 conclusion (pp. 259–260) is read only as Mills (1977) quotes it.

cic_trofimenkoff_1979.note: Re-read 2026-10-14 for the Berger person entry (UBC OJS PDF; pp. 7–20, page numbers from the PDF footers). p. 9: historical writing 'in itself a domain of intellectual history' and its 'concern for survival' (n. 4 cites Cook's two 'La Survivance' essays in The Maple Leaf Forever, pp. 114–40, 141–65, and Windsor in the Literary History of Canada); p. 10: Berger 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists'; 'decidedly masculine affairs'; Shortt and Berger 'have shunned the explicit political commentary of earlier intellectual history'; intellectual history 'will have to take women into account'; pp. 10–11: the first chapter 'simply and pointedly entitled “Men.”'

cic_karr_1989.note: Re-read 2026-10-14 for the Berger person entry (Acadiensis PDF, pp. 158–174, page numbers from running heads). p. 160: 'Ever since Carl Berger used this basic approach in his impressive study of imperialism in the early 1970s, many have adopted his methodology'; p. 161: Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' and 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote'; pp. 162–163: 'over-Canadianization of imperialism' and Carr's 'scavenger hunt for nationalism' (n. 20: Carr 1982; Cole 1970, 1971; Page 1970); p. 167: group biography 'upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method'; p. 168: Berger's premise (Sense of Power, p. 12, per n. 36) and 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe'.

qcreq_rudin_1997.note: Berger passages checked 2026-10-14 in Google Books snippet view (volume Bh5dDMnmFdQC; fragments only). p. 3: Berger's book 'dealt with the situation in English Canada'; p. 4: 'I share Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' and 'I also fundamentally differ with him on several counts. For instance, I do not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth'; p. 6: Berger's view 'is at odds with the one that will be developed in this book'; p. 55: Berger's conclusion that French-Canadian writing was 'remote from some of the chief developments in English-Canadian historiography in the inter-war years'; p. 58: 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair'.

wcreq_kealey_1995.note: Berger passages checked 2026-10-14 in Google Books snippet view (volume RGnUhCZAW9MC; fragments only). Ch. 1 'Writing about Labour', p. 18: Berger's characterization of the 1980s labour-history debate 'has the advantage of offering a non-participant's viewpoint' and 'There is little to argue with in his overall assessment'; p. 30, n. 68: 'Berger's description of the sides conforms closely to Bercuson's own view'. Ch. 3 on Stanley Ryerson (first published in Studies in Political Economy 9, 1982, 103–71, per p. xxiii), p. 84: Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History'.
